title: Simple kinetic method for assessing catalase activity in biological samples
author: Farman, Hadwan
materials: The protocol was summarized in Table 1.

steps.title: Prepare tissue homogenate
steps.instruction: Wash excised liver with 0.9 % (w/v) NaCl solution, homogenize in cold 1.15 % (w/v) KCl using a glass homogenizer, filter the homogenate and dilute 1 : 500 with 50 mM PBS.

steps.title: Add hydrogen peroxide
steps.instruction: Add 2 ml of hydrogen peroxide to each test tube (sample) and to each standard tube.

steps.title: Add sample or water
steps.instruction: Add 1 ml of the catalase‑containing sample to the test tube and 1 ml of distilled water to the standard tube.

steps.title: Incubate reaction
steps.instruction: Vortex the tubes briefly and incubate at 37 °C for 2 min.

steps.title: Quench with ammonium molybdate
steps.instruction: Withdraw 500 µl from each incubated tube and transfer to a clean tube containing 300 µl ammonium molybdate; mix well.

substeps.instruction: Add to tube with 300 µl ammonium molybdate

steps.title: Add pyrogallol red
steps.instruction: Add 3 ml pyrogallol red reagent (1 mmol L⁻¹, pH 7.0) to each tube, mix, and record the zero time as the moment the total PGR volume has been added.

steps.title: Measure absorbance decay
steps.instruction: Within 30 s transfer an appropriate volume of the reaction mixture to a cuvette, record the decrease in absorbance at 545 nm against a distilled‑water blank every few seconds for 0.5–4.5 min after the start of the PGR‑H₂O₂ reaction.

substeps.instruction: Transfer reaction mixture to cuvette within 30 s
Record absorbance at 545 nm against blank from 0.5 to 4.5 min

description: Ammonium molybdate reagent was used to halt the catalase reaction. Ammonium molybdate reacts with H2O2 to form singlet oxygen (1O2) [2]. Subsequently, 1O2 molecules react with reduced PGR to form the oxidized form; as shown in Eqs. (1), (2), and (3). H2O2 dissociation is directly proportional to catalase activity and a decrease in absorbance of the characteristic PGR band (545 nm) at pH 7.0 was used to monitor the rate of PGR oxidation as shown in Figs. 2 and 3.(1)MoO42− + nH2O2 ⇆ MoO4-n(O2)n2−+nH2O(2)MoO4-n(O2)n2−⟶n=2-41O2+MoO6-n(O2)n-22−(3)1O2+ReducedPGR→OxidizedPGRFig. 2Absorption spectra of the different concentrations of PGR, (a) 0.1 mM PGR (b) 0.08 mM PGR (c) 0.05 mM PGR (d) 0.02 mM PGR.Fig 2Fig. 3Variation of the PGR-H2O2-Mo(VI) system as a function to the time. Conditions of reaction: PGR concentration 1 mmol/L, pH 7.0, H2O2 concentration 0.020 mol/L, 2.5 mM Mo(VI) at 30 °C, time interval for each scan 70 s.Fig 3 The catalytic effect of Mo on the oxidation state of PGR with H2O2 has been used previously to determine the concentration of Mo [3].
